title: Johnson County woman pardoned by Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, record expunged | News | paintsvilleherald.com
text:
After more than a decade living under the weight of a felony conviction, Casey Vanhoose was granted a pardon by Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and later saw her record expunged in Johnson Circuit Court.
Vanhoose learned of the pardon on Dec. 19, while at work at The Paintsville Herald, where she is the office manager.
“I cried out praising the Lord after I calmed down,” she said. “I called my husband, my pastor — the two people that I believe made this possible for me — Harry and Greta Meek — my prayer warriors; then my parents and my stepdaughter, Hope.”
The conviction, according to Vanhoose, came during a time when she struggled with self-esteem and looked for acceptance in the wrong places.
“I was a very lonely girl with horrific low self-esteem that got caught up in the wrong crowd so that I would have so-called friends,” Vanhoose said. “Little did I know the devil had my vision and thinking very distorted.”
The record followed her through job interviews and background checks for more than a decade.
“Every single time I went for an interview, they would basically tell me I had the job,” she said. “Then my background would come back, and all of a sudden, they would have a problem with HR and couldn’t hire me. It was like a ghost that haunted me for 13 years.”
Vanhoose said the record also limited her ability to volunteer at her children’s school or participate in school activities that required background checks.
“Job opportunities and volunteering with any school-associated function or sport, you have to have a background check done, which limited me,” she said.
Her record was expunged Jan. 23 by Johnson Circuit Judge John Kevin Holbrook.
“He said that in all his years in politics, before he even became a judge, he had never met anyone whom any governor in Kentucky had ever pardoned,” Vanhoose said.
The expungement, Vanhoose said, allows her to move forward with her life.
“I get to hold my head high and know that I made it,” she said. “I no longer have to live under the embarrassing title of a felon anymore.”
Vanhoose said she plans to continue her education and also hopes to use her experience to help others who are trying to rebuild their lives.
“I have a burning desire to help anyone who has been down or is facing the same road I traveled,” she said. “I want nothing more than to show the broken people how much they are loved.”
Vanhoose credited local attorney Tanner Hesterberg for representing her during the expungement process.
“I truly appreciate Tanner Hesterberg for believing in me and taking on my expungement case,” she said. “He said that when he first met me, he knew I wasn’t the same girl he’d read about in those conviction papers.”
